newsitem.title: THAILAND: New Thai insurance licences spark rush for staff.
newsitem.headline: New Thai insurance licences spark rush for staff.

text.p: Thailand's approval of licences for 28 new insurance companies has sparked a scramble for new sales staff, industry analysts said on Wednesday.
Insurance firms already faced a shortage of trained agents even before the March 25 approval of 12 new life and 16 non-life insurance licences, they said.

"The head-hunting, especially for senior administrators, has started, forcing some existing firms to almost double salaries of experienced staff and to offer more incentives to keep them," said Saravoot Phasuvanichphongse, managing director of Sahawatana Insurance Co Ltd.
Saravoot, president of the General Insurance Association, said the insurance business was growing more than 10 percent a year and that competition was fierce.

Thailand has 67 non-life and 13 life insurance firms. The non-life insurance sector employs about 30,000 full-time staff. The life insurance sector has about 200,000 full-time sales agents and 60,000 administrative staff, according to analysts.

A senior executive at American International Assurance (AIA), which controls about 49 percent of the Thai life insurance market, said about 500 employees had left to join other companies in the past two years.
AIA now has about 30,000 full-time agents and 1,300 administrative staff in Thailand.
The AIA executive, who asked not to be identified, said there were signs that more would leave to join firms offering bigger incentives.
Non-life insurance premiums rose to about 60 billion baht ($2.3 billion) in 1996 from 52 billion baht in 1995.
"Competition is fierce while the market in Thailand is quite small. I think the granting of 28 new insurance licences is too much while the economy isn't bright ...," he said.

Thai authorities last month acted to end a crisis in the financial sector, ordering 10 ailing finance firms to boost capital and raised financial institution provisioning for loans to the depressed property sector.
Saravoot said most affected in the insurance industry by the crisis was the automobile sector as several finance companies were now reluctant to grant credits on hire-purchase cars.
Before the new insurance licences were granted, Saravoot said, owners of life insurance licences sold them for about 350 million baht each against 250 million baht for a non-life licence.
Prices used to be higher for companies with strong goodwill.

New licencees undertaking both life and non-life insurance business are required to incorporate their firms within three months of government approval. They must apply for the licences within six months of setting up business.
A new non-life company must be launched with an initial minimum capital of 300 million baht against 500 million baht for a life insurance company.

Sukhathep Chansrichawla, president and chief executive of Thai Prasit Insurance Co Ltd, said he believed some of the firms obtaining both life and non-life licences may try to seek more foreign partners.
Thai law allows foreign investors to hold up to 49 percent in insurance companies.
